title: 08. Multi-Agent & Patterns: QUERY TRANSFORMATION TECHNIQUES
summary: Query transformation is the art of turning a raw user query into one or more optimized search queries BEFORE hitting the vector DB. > Users write queries the way they think. Vector DBs need queries that match how documents are written.

sections.title: What Is Query Transformation?
sections.body:
> **Query transformation is the art of turning a raw user query into one or more optimized search queries BEFORE hitting the vector DB.**
> Users write queries the way they think. Vector DBs need queries that match how documents are written. Transformation bridges this gap.

sections.title: All Query Transformation Techniques
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           8 QUERY TRANSFORMATION TECHNIQUES                     │
├────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────── │
│ #  │  Technique               │  When to Use                    │
├────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────── │
│ 1  │  Query Expansion         │  Short / vague queries          │
│ 2  │  Query Rewriting         │  Poorly worded queries          │
```

sections.title: Technique 1 — Query Expansion
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               TECHNIQUE 1: QUERY EXPANSION                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROBLEM IT SOLVES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  User query: "ML overfitting"
  Vector search: finds docs with "ML overfitting" literally
  Misses: "model generalization", "regularization techniques",
           "training vs validation loss", "bias-variance tradeoff"
  All of these ANSWER the user's question but use different words!

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Original:  "ML overfitting"
  Expanded:  "ML overfitting OR machine learning overfitting
              OR model overfitting regularization
              OR bias variance tradeoff
              OR training validation loss gap
              OR L1 L2 regularization dropout"

  Expand with:
  • Synonyms:    "ML" → "machine learning", "artificial intelligence"
  • Related terms: "overfitting" → "regularization", "generalization"
  • Acronym expansion: "NLP" → "natural language processing"
  • Domain vocabulary: add field-specific terminology

  BEFORE EXPANSION:                AFTER EXPANSION:
  ─────────────────────────        ───────────────────────────────
  Found: 3 docs (exact match)      Found: 12 docs (semantic match)
  Top result score: 0.82           Top result score: 0.91
  Answer quality: incomplete       Answer quality: comprehensive

  WHEN TO USE:
  ✅ Short queries (< 5 words)
  ✅ Technical queries with acronyms
  ✅ When recall matters more than precision
  ✅ Domain-specific knowledge bases
```

sections.title: Technique 2 — Query Rewriting
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               TECHNIQUE 2: QUERY REWRITING                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROBLEM IT SOLVES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Users write queries in CASUAL language.
  Documents use TECHNICAL / FORMAL language.

  User query:    "why does my python code eat up all memory"
  Document text: "Python memory leak causes and prevention strategies"

  The words don't match even though it's the SAME question!

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Casual:    "why does my python code eat up all memory"
  Rewritten: "Python memory leak diagnosis and prevention"

  Casual:    "how do i make chatgpt smarter for my use case"
  Rewritten: "LLM fine-tuning and prompt engineering techniques"

  Casual:    "vector database too slow"
  Rewritten: "vector database query optimization and performance tuning"

  Rewriting NORMALIZES:
  • Casual → formal language
  • Question form → keyword/topic form
  • First person → general description
  • Vague → specific terminology
  • Colloquial → technical vocabulary

  CONVERSATION CONTEXT REWRITING:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Turn 1: "Tell me about Python decorators"
  Turn 2: "How do I use them with async functions?"

  "them" = ??? (the vector DB doesn't know what "them" refers to!)

  Rewritten: "How to use Python decorators with async functions"
  ↑ Now the query is SELF-CONTAINED and searchable ✅

  This is called COREFERENCE RESOLUTION in rewriting.
```

sections.title: Technique 3 — HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               TECHNIQUE 3: HyDE                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ALREADY COVERED IN LAYER 7 — quick recap:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Instead of embedding the QUERY:
  → Generate what the PERFECT ANSWER would look like
  → Embed THAT (much richer signal)
  → Search with the hypothetical document's embedding

  Query:   "memory management in agents"          ← 4 words, vague
  HyDoc:   "AI agents use multiple memory types.  ← 60 words, rich
            Short-term memory stores recent turns.
            Long-term memory uses vector databases.
            Working memory manages active task info..."
  Search:  HyDoc embedding finds much better matches ✅
```

sections.title: Technique 4 — Step-Back Prompting
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               TECHNIQUE 4: STEP-BACK PROMPTING                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROBLEM IT SOLVES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Some questions are TOO SPECIFIC to find good answers.
  We need to "zoom out" to find the foundational concepts first,
  then apply them to the specific question.

  SPECIFIC QUESTION:
  "Why does GPT-4o give different answers with temperature=0.9
   vs temperature=0.1 for coding tasks?"

  If you search this directly: probably finds nothing useful.
  The question is too specific for most docs to directly address.

  STEP BACK → find the PRINCIPLE first:
  "What does the temperature parameter do in LLMs?"
  → Finds: "Temperature controls randomness in token sampling.
             Lower = more deterministic. Higher = more creative."
  → NOW we can answer the specific question!

  THE ALGORITHM:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Original: "Why does GPT-4o give different answers with temp=0.9
             vs temp=0.1 for coding tasks?"

  Step-Back: "What is temperature in LLMs?"
                    │
                    ▼
             Search for general principle
                    │
                    ▼
             Found: "Temperature controls sampling randomness"
                    │
                    ▼
  Answer original question USING the general knowledge ✅

  MORE EXAMPLES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Specific: "Why does my RAG fail on 5-word queries?"
  Step-Back: "What affects vector search quality?" → broad principle

  Specific: "How do I fix KeyError in my LangChain agent?"
  Step-Back: "How do LangChain agents handle tool outputs?" → principle

  Specific: "My Pinecone index is slow after 10M vectors"
  Step-Back: "How do vector databases scale?" → broad principle

  WHEN TO USE:
  ✅ "Why does X happen?" questions → step back to principles
  ✅ Debugging-type questions → step back to how system works
  ✅ Very specific technical questions
  ✅ When direct search returns no results
```

sections.title: Technique 5 — Sub-Query Decomposition
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               TECHNIQUE 5: SUB-QUERY DECOMPOSITION              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROBLEM IT SOLVES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Complex questions need information from MULTIPLE sources/topics.
  A single query can't get everything at once.

  COMPLEX QUESTION:
  "Compare LangChain and LlamaIndex for building a production
   RAG system — which handles chunking, retrieval, and
   cost optimization better?"

  This ONE question contains FIVE sub-questions:
  1. What is LangChain's approach to chunking?
  2. What is LlamaIndex's approach to chunking?
  3. How does LangChain handle retrieval?
  4. How does LlamaIndex handle retrieval?
  5. What cost optimization features does each have?

  DECOMPOSITION ALGORITHM:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Original question
         │
         ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LLM: "Break this into independent sub-questions"   │
  └──────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                                     │
         ┌───────────┬───────────────┼───────────────┐
         ▼           ▼               ▼               ▼
      Sub-Q 1    Sub-Q 2          Sub-Q 3         Sub-Q 4
    "LangChain  "LlamaIndex    "LangChain      "LlamaIndex
     chunking"   chunking"      retrieval"      retrieval"
         │           │               │               │
         ▼           ▼               ▼               ▼
      Search      Search          Search          Search
         │           │               │               │
         └───────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┘
                                 │
                                 ▼
                    Combine all results
                                 │
                                 ▼
                    Answer original complex question ✅

  SEQUENTIAL vs PARALLEL DECOMPOSITION:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  PARALLEL (independent sub-questions):
  All sub-queries search at the same time → Fast
  "What is X?" + "What is Y?" + "How does Z work?"

  SEQUENTIAL (dependent sub-questions):
  Answer sub-Q1 first, use result to form sub-Q2
  "Who created X?" → "What else did that person build?"
  (This is Multi-Hop RAG from Layer 7)
```

sections.title: Technique 6 — Query Routing
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               TECHNIQUE 6: QUERY ROUTING                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROBLEM IT SOLVES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Different queries need different data sources.
  Not everything is in the vector DB.

  Query: "What is today's stock price of AAPL?"
  → NOT in vector DB (real-time data needed) → route to API

  Query: "How do I use LangChain agents?"
  → IN vector DB (technical docs) → route to vector DB

  Query: "What did the CEO say last week?"
  → NOT in vector DB (recent news) → route to web search

  THE ROUTING MAP:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   USER QUERY                           │
  └────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
                    ┌──────────────────────┐
                    │   QUERY CLASSIFIER   │
                    └──────────┬───────────┘
                               │
          ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          │                    │                    │
          ▼                    ▼                    ▼
  [Technical Docs]     [Real-Time Data]     [Database]
  → Vector DB          → Web Search API    → SQL Query
  → "How does X work?" → "Current price"   → "Show orders"
  → "Best practices"   → "Latest news"     → "User history"
  → "Code examples"    → "Live weather"    → "Sales report"

  ROUTING STRATEGIES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. KEYWORD ROUTING (fastest):
     "price", "stock", "weather" → real-time API
     "how", "what is", "explain" → vector DB
     "show", "list", "count"     → SQL database

  2. LLM ROUTING (most accurate):
     Ask LLM to classify the query type
     LLM returns: "technical_doc" | "real_time" | "database"

  3. EMBEDDING ROUTING (semantic):
     Compare query embedding to "route prototype" embeddings
     Route to source with highest semantic similarity
```

sections.title: Technique 7 — Multi-Query Generation
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               TECHNIQUE 7: MULTI-QUERY GENERATION               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROBLEM IT SOLVES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  One query = one angle of view.
  Different phrasings of the same question find DIFFERENT docs.

  "How to speed up RAG retrieval?"
  "RAG latency optimization techniques"
  "Making vector search faster in production"
  "Reducing response time in retrieval augmented generation"

  → Each finds DIFFERENT relevant documents!
  → Combined, they find MORE than any single query.

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Original: "How to make my RAG system faster?"

  Generated variants (4 perspectives):
  1. "RAG performance optimization strategies"          ← technical
  2. "Reducing vector database query latency"           ← specific
  3. "Improving retrieval speed augmented generation"   ← verbose
  4. "Caching and indexing for faster RAG systems"      ← solutions

  Run ALL 4 searches → get 4 × top-10 = 40 docs
  Deduplicate → ~25 unique docs
  Rerank with RRF → top 5
  Generate answer from richer context ✅

  COMPARED TO SINGLE QUERY:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Single query:  10 docs → some relevant, some not
  Multi-query:   25 unique docs → more perspectives covered
  Answer:        More complete, fewer blind spots

  HOW MANY VARIANTS?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2-3: Good balance of coverage vs cost
  4-5: Maximum coverage (Fusion RAG)
  1:   No benefit (same as baseline)
  >5:  Diminishing returns + high cost
```

sections.title: Technique 8 — Contextual Query Compression
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               TECHNIQUE 8: CONTEXTUAL COMPRESSION               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROBLEM IT SOLVES:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  A retrieved document might be 2000 words.
  Only 50 words of it actually answer the question.
  The other 1950 words are NOISE in the LLM's context window.
  More noise = worse answers + higher token cost.

  ORIGINAL DOC (2000 words retrieved):
  "Python was created by Guido van Rossum in 1991...
   [500 words of Python history]
   ...Python 3.0 introduced breaking changes...
   [300 words about Python 2 vs 3]
   ...Memory management in Python uses reference counting.
   Memory leaks occur when circular references prevent
   garbage collection. Use tracemalloc to detect leaks.
   The gc module can force collection of cycles...
   [50 words — the ACTUAL answer]
   ...Python's GIL affects multithreading...
   [600 words about GIL]"

  QUERY: "How to detect memory leaks in Python?"

  COMPRESSED DOC (50 words — only the answer):
  "Memory leaks occur when circular references prevent
   garbage collection. Use tracemalloc to detect leaks.
   The gc module can force collection of cycles."

  RESULT:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Before compression: 2000 tokens per doc × 5 docs = 10,000 tokens
  After compression:  50 tokens per doc × 5 docs  =    250 tokens
  Cost savings: 97.5% ✅
  Answer quality: BETTER (less noise) ✅
  Latency: FASTER (fewer tokens to process) ✅

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  For each retrieved doc:
  Ask LLM: "Extract ONLY the parts that answer: [query]
             Discard everything else."
  → Returns compressed, query-focused excerpt
```
